title: I can't stop looking at porn
seoTitle: How to Stop Watching Porn: Faith, Shame, and Real Help
description: Can't stop looking at porn, or found it on a spouse's or child's phone? What Scripture says, why it's so hard, and real steps out of hiding.
summary: For the one who keeps going back, and the spouse or parent who found out: shame named, and a real way out of hiding.
askedAs: What does the Bible say about pornography
I found porn on my son's phone
answer: You've told yourself it was the last time, maybe more times than you can count, and here you are again, clearing the history and feeling sick about it. Maybe it started years ago, before you understood what it would do to you. Now it finds you when you're lonely, bored, stressed, or can't sleep, and the shame afterward pulls you back. You aren't beyond God's reach, and you aren't the only one. You've tried beating this alone and in secret; the way out starts with telling one person the truth. If the shame has turned into thoughts of ending your life, call or text 988 now. And if you're the spouse who found it, this is a betrayal and it isn't your fault. There's help below for you, and for the parent who found it on a teenager's phone.
happening:
It usually runs in a pattern you could draw from memory. A long day, a lonely evening, a flash of boredom or stress, and the phone is right there. You tell yourself it'll only be a minute, and then an hour is gone. Afterward comes the crash: disgust, the deleted history, the promise that this was the last time, the fear of being found out. For a while you try harder, and then the pressure builds and it happens again. You can start to feel like two people, the one your family knows and the one who's awake at one in the morning. For some it started young, by accident, long before they had words for it. And it isn't only men. Women struggle with this too, and they can feel doubly alone when the church talks as if they don't.

The common explanations each hold part of the truth. Anything that rewards us quickly and reliably can become a habit that's hard to break. Some counselors call what follows an addiction; others speak of compulsive sexual behavior, and professionals don't all agree on the label. This page can't diagnose you, and the label matters less than an honest answer to one question: have you been able to stop when you've tried? The spiritual account is true as well. Jesus called lust adultery of the heart, and this is a real moral struggle, not a quirk of wiring.

What each account can miss is the rest of you. Treat it only as a brain habit, and you lose sight of the heart and of the people on the screen. Treat it only as sin, and the answer shrinks to *try harder and pray more*, which many sincere Christians have tried for years without getting free. Both can miss the shame. The self-disgust after a fall feels like holiness, but it sends you back into hiding, and hiding is where this grows. Condemnation feeds it, and so does easy reassurance, *everybody does it, it's harmless*, because that leaves you alone with it too.

And if you're reading this because you found it, on a husband's laptop, a wife's phone, or your son's tablet, you're carrying something too: shock, anger, grief, and questions about yourself you shouldn't have to ask. There's a part of this page written for you.

scripture.intro: Scripture is more honest about this than most of us have been. It names the look as well as the act, keeps a king's confession in its prayer book, and treats the body as something God bought and means to raise. Each passage is read where it stands: who said it, to whom, and why.

passages.text: You have heard that it was said, ‘Do not commit adultery.’ But I tell you that anyone who looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.
passages.reading: Jesus said this in the Sermon on the Mount, to crowds who had heard the commandment and could keep it by staying out of the wrong bed. He moves it inward, from the act to the look that wants to use a person, and that leaves every one of us exposed. Then come the hardest lines: “If your right eye causes you to sin, gouge it out and throw it away” (Matthew 5:29), and the same for the right hand. This is no call to harm your body. Jesus has just said that lust lives in the heart, and in the same sermon he pictures a beam in a man's eye (Matthew 7:3); he exaggerates on purpose so you'll see how serious this is. Cut off whatever feeds it. If you've had thoughts of hurting yourself over this, tell someone tonight, or call or text 988. And if you're the spouse who found out, you aren't overreacting. Jesus used the word adultery.

passages.text: Have mercy on me, O God, according to Your loving devotion; according to Your great compassion, blot out my transgressions. Wash me clean of my iniquity and cleanse me from my sin. For I know my transgressions, and my sin is always before me. ... Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. Cast me not away from Your presence; take not Your Holy Spirit from me. Restore to me the joy of Your salvation, and sustain me with a willing spirit.
passages.reading: The psalm bears David's name, and its heading sets it after the prophet Nathan confronted him over Bathsheba. That story began with a look. From the palace roof the king “saw a woman bathing” (2 Samuel 11:2), sent for her, and then arranged her husband's death to cover what he'd done. He kept it hidden for months, until Nathan said, “You are that man!” (2 Samuel 12:7). What the psalm asks for is a clean heart, and the Hebrew verb for create is the one Genesis uses when God creates the heavens and the earth (Genesis 1:1). You can't manufacture a clean heart any more than you can make a world, but you can ask the One who can. “My sin is always before me” (Psalm 51:3) is what shame feels like, the replay that won't stop, and here it's said to God, who “will not despise” a broken and contrite heart (Psalm 51:17).

passages.text: Flee from sexual immorality. Every other sin a man can commit is outside his body, but he who sins sexually sins against his own body. Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have received from God? You are not your own; you were bought at a price. Therefore glorify God with your body.
passages.reading: Paul's warnings suggest that some men in the church at Corinth were visiting prostitutes and defending it with slogans, which the BSB sets in quotation marks: “Everything is permissible for me” and “Food for the stomach and the stomach for food” (1 Corinthians 6:12-13). On that view the body is only appetite. Our screens say the same: it's private, it's only looking, nobody gets hurt. Paul answers that the body is meant “for the Lord” and that God, who raised Jesus, “will raise us also” (1 Corinthians 6:13-14), so the body matters forever. Then he names a price. Pornography comes from pornē, the Greek word Paul uses for a prostitute in verse 15, and pornē is related to a verb for selling. Porn is still a market in bodies. Against it Paul sets another purchase: you were bought, at the cost of Christ's own life. Shame treats your body as something to despise. God paid for it.

passages.text: What a wretched man I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death? Thanks be to God, through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, with my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin. Therefore, there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
passages.reading: Just before this cry, Paul describes a war many readers know from the inside: “For what I want to do, I do not do. But what I hate, I do” (Romans 7:15). Christians have long disagreed about whether he's describing life before Christ or the struggle that goes on after it, and faithful readers stand on both sides. Either way, the chapter turns on a person, “Thanks be to God, through Jesus Christ our Lord!” (Romans 7:25), and then on a verdict that holds for those who are in Christ even while the struggle goes on. Shame says you are what you did last night. The gospel says that in Christ you are his, and the fight you're in is one you wage from forgiveness, not for it.

whyHard:
The easy explanation is that this is a modern problem, and the internet did it. There's truth in that. No generation before ours had an endless, free, private supply within reach at every hour, built by people who study how to keep you clicking. But the desire, and the hiding, are as old as we are. In the Bible's first story of sin, the man tells God, “I was afraid because I was naked; so I hid myself” (Genesis 3:10). David's fall began with a look from a roof. Augustine, whose Confessions tell of his conversion in a garden in Milan in 386, remembered praying for chastity and asking God not to grant it yet, and the words that finally turned him were Paul's: “make no provision for the desires of the flesh” (Romans 13:14). What's new is the provision, and it's in your pocket.

Lust is only part of the story. Notice when it comes: at the end of a lonely night, a dull afternoon, a day that went badly. It offers relief without risk, closeness with no one who could turn you away, being wanted without being known. It's a counterfeit of something good. Before the hiding, “the man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed” (Genesis 2:25), fully seen and fully safe. Porn sells the reverse, the chance to look without ever being seen. And because shame makes us hide, and porn is a place to hide, a fall deepens the shame that drives the next one.

The church hasn't made this easier. For a generation, many churches taught sexual purity mostly as rules and warnings, treated the body as a problem, and made this a sin almost no one would mention in a small group. We handed people a list of what not to do and said little about desire, grace, and the goodness of the body, so people hid in the pews as well as online. I'm a pastor, and I don't get to stand outside that failure. Some researchers have found that people who believe porn is wrong but keep watching it are especially likely to feel addicted to it, and they propose that the moral conflict itself, and not only how much someone watches, feeds that feeling. We should take that seriously, because shame has fed this cycle. But porn still trains desire to take without giving, and the people on the screen are real, with names and families, and you can't know what was done to put them there.

Rules can't reach this, and shame drives it deeper. What reaches it is the thing porn was built to spare you: being seen. When the first couple hid, God came looking and called, “Where are you?” (Genesis 3:9), and before he sent them from the garden he clothed them himself (Genesis 3:21). Jesus was stripped and crucified in public view, and he “endured the cross, scorning its shame” (Hebrews 12:2), so that people who hide could come out and not be thrown away. That's why confession loosens what willpower couldn't. Porn offers a way to look without being seen. The gospel offers something harder and better: to be seen completely, and kept.

thisWeek.intro: One week won't undo years, but it can hold a few honest steps out of hiding. Start with the first; it matters most. If the shame has turned into thoughts of ending your life, start instead by calling or texting 988 tonight, and tell someone near you.

steps.title: Tell one person the truth
steps.body: Choose one person this week and tell them the plain truth. Pick someone mature who will keep your confidence and won't flinch or shrug it off: a pastor, a counselor, an older friend of your own sex, or, if you're a teenager, a parent or another adult you trust. The letter of James puts confession beside healing: “confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed” (James 5:16). If you're married, your spouse deserves the truth too; see the questions below on telling them well.

steps.title: Get the phone out of your bedroom
steps.body: Tonight, charge your phone outside the room where you sleep. Then change the setup as well as your resolve: turn on the content restrictions built into your devices, let someone else hold the passcode, and delete the apps, accounts, and searches that lead you there. It's a plain way to obey what Jesus meant about cutting off what causes you to sin (Matthew 5:30). Don't prop the door open and then pray you won't walk through it.

steps.title: Learn your hour
steps.body: Think back over the last few times and write down when it happened, where you were, and what you felt beforehand: lonely, bored, angry, stressed, rejected, exhausted. You may find it's the same hour and the same room again and again. Then plan for that hour. Go to bed at a set time, stay out of that room, and spend your weakest hours around other people.

steps.title: Plan the next ten minutes
steps.body: Decide now what you'll do when the urge comes, because you won't think clearly in the moment. Get up and leave the room. Go outside, or go where people are. Text your person a word you've agreed on. Pray one honest sentence: *Lord, I want this, and I want to want you more. Help me.* The urge will insist it's permanent. It passes. When his master's wife grabbed him, Joseph “escaped and ran outside” (Genesis 39:12).

steps.title: Ask for accountability, not surveillance
steps.body: Ask your person for accountability, which means someone who knows the truth and asks real questions, not someone watching your screen. Set a regular time, weekly at first, and let them ask: *When was the last time? What was going on before it? What aren't you telling me?* Tell the truth before you're asked. Filters and reports can help with the setup, but they can't make you honest. And don't make your spouse your monitor; they were the one wronged, and they need care of their own.

steps.title: If you fall, get up the same day
steps.body: If you fall this week, don't let one night become a lost month. Shame will say you've already blown it, so you might as well keep going. Refuse it. Tell God the truth that night, tell your person the next day, and look at what led up to it. The book of Micah gives God's people words for a fall that was their own fault: “Though I have fallen, I will arise” (Micah 7:8).

moreHelp.body:
This is more than a pastoral matter when you've tried to stop and can't, when it's escalating or costing you sleep, work, money, or your marriage, or when it's tangled up with depression, anxiety, old wounds, or thoughts of ending your life. A pastor can pray with you and keep you honest; a licensed counselor can help you see what's driving it and change the pattern. You may need both.

Look for a licensed counselor (a professional counselor, marriage and family therapist, clinical social worker, or psychologist) with training and experience in compulsive sexual behavior, and ask about that directly. If you want a Christian counselor, ask about license and training as well as faith. Get names from your doctor, your insurance company's directory, or a pastor who knows the counselors near you, then confirm the license on your state licensing board's website. For a teenager, start with the family doctor or the school counselor. If you're the spouse, find a counselor of your own who understands betrayal. And if what you carry includes sexual abuse, now or long ago, RAINN's hotline in the help block is there for that.
signs: You've tried to stop again and again, and you can't.
It takes more and more of your time, or you're seeking out things that disturb you.
It's costing you sleep, work, money, or your marriage, or it has moved from a screen toward real people.
Anything you've seen or found shows someone under eighteen. That's a crime; report it to the police, or if you're a teenager, tell a parent or another adult you trust, who can report it.
Someone hurt you sexually, now or when you were young.
You're afraid of your spouse, or you're being pressured or forced into sex.
The shame has turned into hopelessness or thoughts of ending your life. Call or text 988 now.
moreHelp.firstCall: You can say it plainly: *I've been struggling with pornography for a long time, and I can't stop on my own. Do you work with compulsive sexual behavior?* A good counselor won't be shocked. Ask whether they're licensed in your state, how much experience they have with this, what they charge, and whether they take your insurance. If you're the spouse, you can say, *I just found out my husband has been hiding pornography, and I need help for myself.*
moreHelp.cost: Counseling isn't cheap, but cost shouldn't keep you stuck. Ask about sliding-scale fees, and look into community mental health centers and university training clinics, where supervised graduate students see clients for less. Many employers offer an employee assistance program with a few free, confidential sessions. Your church may have a benevolence fund; ask. Many church and community recovery groups meet at no cost.

helping.body:
If you're the spouse who found out, start here. Rage, numbness, nausea, the urge to check every device in the house: none of it means you're overreacting. This is a betrayal, and it isn't your fault. You don't have to decide tonight what happens to your marriage, and you don't have to become your spouse's counselor or monitor. You need care of your own, one friend who will keep your confidence and a counselor who understands betrayal. If you're afraid of your spouse, or they pressure or force you sexually, that's more than a porn problem; reach the Domestic Violence Hotline in the help block.

If you're a parent who found porn on your teenager's phone, breathe before you speak. The first ten minutes can teach your child whether it's safe to bring you something hard, and the last question below walks through that conversation. I'm raising five sons, and I'd rather they hear the truth about this from me than from a screen.

If a friend confesses this to you, thank them, and don't act shocked or shrug it off. Paul told the Galatians to restore someone caught in a trespass “with a spirit of gentleness,” and added, “But watch yourself, or you also may be tempted” (Galatians 6:1). Keep their confidence unless someone is in danger or a child is involved. Pastors, if a minor is being harmed or exploited, you may be a mandated reporter; the rules vary by state, so learn yours. This isn't legal advice.
say: Thank you for telling me. I'm not going anywhere.
This is serious, and you're not beyond help.
What's usually going on right before it happens?
Can I check in with you on Friday?
What happened to you is not your fault.
I love you, and you can always tell me the truth.
dontSay: Every guy does it. It's no big deal.
If your spouse met your needs, this wouldn't happen.
Why were you looking at his phone?
helping.next: Check in again within a few days, and keep checking; this struggle feeds on silence. Ask how it's safe to reach them, since a spouse, parent, or roommate may see their messages. Help with one concrete step, like finding a counselor or sitting with them while they make the call. If you're supporting a betrayed spouse, don't carry messages between the two of them or rush their decisions. Pray for them by name, and keep coming back.

prayer:
Lord, you already know where I was last night and what I looked at, and how many times I've promised you it was the last. I'm tired of hiding, and I'm afraid of being found.

When you come looking for me, as you came looking in the garden, don't let me hide among the trees. Create in me a clean heart, because I can't make one. Give me the nerve to tell one person the truth, and the humility to keep telling it.

Have mercy on the people on those screens. They're somebody's children, and they're yours. Have mercy on anyone I've wounded by what I hid, and don't let me excuse it.

When shame tells me I'm beyond you, remind me that you bought this body and mean to raise it. When I fall, lift me the same day. Teach me to want what's real.

Amen.

faq.a: Yes, and it helps to be precise about why. Jesus said that “anyone who looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:28), so Scripture treats lust as a matter of faithfulness, not a harmless private habit. Porn also uses real people whose stories you can't know. But the Bible that names the sin also names its cure: “there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). Calling it sin isn't meant to crush you. It's meant to bring you into the light, where you can be forgiven and begin to change.

This isn't a question the creeds settle, and faithful Christians answer it differently. Some hold that it's always wrong, because God made sexual desire for the union in which two “will become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24); turning it back on yourself bends a gift meant for another, and it's seldom free of lust. Their comfort is clarity, and the conviction that your longings mean something too good to spend alone. Others hold that it isn't sin in itself, since Scripture never names it, and they judge it by what Scripture does name: lust (Matthew 5:28), and Paul's test, “I will not be mastered by anything” (1 Corinthians 6:12). Their comfort is freedom from guilt Scripture doesn't assign, so the real fight, against lust and against being mastered, gets your full attention. Both agree that porn is wrong, that self-disgust isn't the same as repentance, and that no one is beyond grace. Talk it through with a pastor you trust, or with a parent if you're a teenager.

faq.q: I keep relapsing. Will God keep forgiving me?
faq.a: Yes. The first letter of John was written to believers “so that you will not sin,” and the next words are “But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate before the Father” (1 John 2:1). God's mercy doesn't run out because you've needed it again: “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9). What wears out is the strategy of fighting alone. So confess again, and then change something: tell another person, change the setup, see a counselor. Forgiveness is free, and it's meant to lead you somewhere new.

Your spouse deserves the truth, and a marriage can't be rebuilt on something still hidden. Tell them, but not on impulse and not alone. Talk first with a counselor or pastor about how to tell the whole truth at once, its full extent without needless detail, since truth that comes out in pieces reopens the wound each time. Don't minimize it, and don't ask your spouse to carry your guilt or be your accountability partner. Expect grief and anger, and let trust return at whatever pace they can manage. “He who conceals his sins will not prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them will find mercy” (Proverbs 28:13).

faq.q: My husband watches porn. Is it my fault?
faq.a: No. You didn't cause this, and you can't fix it by changing your body, your clothes, or your sex life. The letter of James says, “each one is tempted when by his own evil desires he is lured away and enticed” (James 1:14). Your hurt isn't an overreaction; Jesus spoke of lust as adultery in the heart, so it's right to call this a betrayal, whichever spouse it is. You don't have to decide tonight what happens next, and whether this can end a marriage is a question faithful churches answer differently. Get support of your own, a trusted friend and a counselor who understands betrayal. If you're afraid of him, or he pressures you sexually, call the Domestic Violence Hotline in the help block.

faq.q: I found porn on my son's phone. What should I do?
faq.a: Stay calm, and don't lead with punishment. Talk when you're steady, alone with your son or daughter, and start with love: *I found this. I love you, and we're going to talk about it.* Ask what happened before you assume; children can stumble onto porn long before they go looking. Explain what porn gets wrong about people, and don't shame their body or their curiosity. Keep devices in shared spaces at night and use the parental controls you have, but aim for a child who will tell you the truth. If they can't stop, find a counselor. If anything you found shows someone under eighteen, that's a crime, and it should be reported to the police.

slots.note: Where James lands on masturbation, in his own words, and the tradition his view comes from. The answer to 'Is masturbation a sin?' gives each view its strongest verse and its real comfort, and deliberately does not land.

As a father of five sons who was raised without a father, James could add, in his own words, how he talks with his sons about pornography and the body, or what he wishes someone had told him as a boy. Only from James; the parent paragraph stands without it.

James came to faith from atheism. If he wants to, a few sentences on how the secular account of desire and the Christian account of the body looked to him before and after would meet the skeptic in this section. Only from James; the section stands without it.

Whether James holds that a spouse's hidden pornography use can be grounds for ending a marriage, in his own words, and the tradition his view comes from. The answer to 'My husband watches porn. Is it my fault?' says only that faithful churches answer this differently, and deliberately does not land.

Any counselors, recovery groups, or ministries near Fenton that James trusts to name for compulsive sexual behavior or for betrayed spouses, and whether First Baptist Church of Fenton has a confidential group or a protocol when a spouse or a parent discloses this. Only from James.

The Greek word for prostitute in 1 Corinthians 6:15-16 is pornē.

sources.claim: The research the page describes: in the Pornography Problems due to Moral Incongruence model, people who morally disapprove of pornography but use it are more likely to report feeling addicted to it, and the authors propose that this moral incongruence, and not only the amount of use, contributes to those self-perceived problems; their systematic review and meta-analysis found moral incongruence consistently associated with self-perceived problems. The page claims only this. The paper does not argue that shame does more harm than pornography, and the page no longer says it does.
